segments.title: Opening of Reel 1 and microphone setup
segments.summary: Interviewer and Tyler set up the microphones and begin the 1996 interview.

segments.title: Full name, the O'en middle name, and parents
segments.summary: Tyler explains the spelling of his middle name and names his parents, Virgil Tyler and Leona Maud Beverly.

segments.title: Birth in 1925 and the eleven brothers and sisters
segments.summary: Youngest of eleven surviving children, born December 5, 1925; he lists his siblings in order.

segments.title: Growing up on Bienville in the Fourth Ward
segments.summary: He describes the Bienville Street neighborhood near St. Louis Cemetery and who still lived at home.

segments.title: Parents' work, the Depression and the household
segments.summary: His father was a laborer, his mother mostly a housewife; the Depression barely touched him and relatives came and went at 2119 Bienville.

segments.title: Radio, the player piano and movie musicals
segments.summary: Early musical influence came from the radio, a pumped player piano and 1930s movie musicals rather than family musicians.

segments.title: Segregated neighborhood movie theaters
segments.summary: He names the Arcade and the downtown theaters and who could sit where.

segments.title: WPA band at McDonogh 37 and Sam Lee's circular breathing
segments.summary: He heard the WPA band at his grade school and was awed by saxophonist Sam Lee's circular breathing.

segments.title: Schools attended and no music training before the service
segments.summary: He lists his schools and says he did not start playing until after the army.

segments.title: Phonographs, dance halls, truck advertising and second lines
segments.summary: He had no phonograph but went to dance halls, saw funeral second lines, and describes bands advertising dances from trucks.

segments.title: Seeing touring bands at the San Jacinto dance hall
segments.summary: He describes the Gypsy Tea Room and the San Jacinto hall, where he saw name bands, and how it was laid out.

segments.title: Drafted in 1945 and re-upping after the war
segments.summary: Drafted in January 1945 and trained as a surgical technician; after the war ended he re-upped for a year and went home on furlough.

segments.title: Marrying Leona Ross and Germany with the ambulance outfit
segments.summary: He married his first wife Leona Ross in 1945, spent about six months in Bremerhaven, and returned to a project apartment near the Nevilles.

segments.title: Learning of Grunewald through the G.I. Bill and joining Clyde Kerr's band
segments.summary: He bought a saxophone, enrolled at Grunewald School of Music on the G.I. Bill, and within six months joined Clyde Kerr's band and the black union.

segments.title: Learning to read and arrange; Earl Palmer
segments.summary: He recalls early reading and arranging mistakes and his childhood acquaintance with drummer Earl Palmer, whom he urged to attend Grunewald.

segments.title: Segregated Grunewald: the band upstairs
segments.summary: Black and white students were taught separately at Grunewald, and white students sneaked upstairs to hear the black students' band.

segments.title: Teachers at Grunewald
segments.summary: He names teachers Willie Humphrey, Clyde Kerr, Shirley Chatters Bloom, Sun Johnson and Louis Cottrell.

segments.title: Daily routine, G.I. pay and buying his saxophone
segments.summary: Students studied theory, harmony and arranging all day on a government monthly allowance; he bought his first instrument.

segments.title: Playing in Clyde Kerr's band and picking up the saxophone quickly
segments.summary: He describes Kerr's small band and how teachers marveled at his solos, which he credits to starting late and focusing.

segments.title: No side job and finishing the G.I. program
segments.summary: He did not need a side job while on the government allowance and received a certificate when his allotted time ended.

segments.chapter: Dew Drop and the name Red
segments.title: Early gigs: stranded on the Roy Brown tour, then the Dew Drop show band
segments.summary: He stood in for Earl Barnes on a road tour that left the band stranded in Port Arthur, then played shows at the Dew Drop.

segments.chapter: Dew Drop and the name Red
segments.title: Pay and atmosphere at the Dew Drop
segments.summary: The Dew Drop paid about eight dollars, was a sit-down club, and drinks were cheap; the room later moved to the back.

segments.chapter: Dew Drop and the name Red
segments.title: The Dew Drop's rooms and owner Frank Pannier
segments.summary: He describes the front and back rooms and Frank Pannier, who owned the club and hotel and treated him well.

segments.chapter: Dew Drop and the name Red
segments.title: How he got the name Red and being called Alvin
segments.summary: He explains that Red refers to light skin in black culture, how billing as Red Tyler made it stick, and who still calls him Alvin.

segments.chapter: Dave Bartholomew band and early recording
segments.title: Joining Dave Bartholomew's band
segments.summary: Through Earl Palmer he joined Bartholomew's band, which played rhythm and blues, stock arrangements, carnival balls and out-of-town dances.

segments.chapter: Dave Bartholomew band and early recording
segments.title: First recordings with Bartholomew, Smiley Lewis and Fats Domino
segments.summary: He recalls his first recordings, a split Fats Domino session with Jewel King where he played the solo, and learning the disc-recording process.

segments.chapter: Dave Bartholomew band and early recording
segments.title: Radio remotes from J&M and full-time musician
segments.summary: They did unpaid Sunday radio remotes from the studio behind J&M Music Store; music was his full-time work.

segments.chapter: Dave Bartholomew band and early recording
segments.title: Death of his first wife and mother in 1951
segments.summary: His wife, who had a heart condition, dropped dead near his mother's house and the shock killed his mother; Earl Palmer pulled him back to the club.

segments.title: Session work through Cosmo and the move to baritone
segments.summary: Cosmo Matassa called the core of Bartholomew's band for sessions; he switched to baritone alongside Lee Allen on tenor.

segments.title: Lee Allen: first sight in Denver and his background
segments.summary: He first saw Lee Allen at a USO in Denver, and says Allen came to New Orleans on a basketball scholarship and played with Paul Gayten.

segments.title: The so-called clique and pride in hits
segments.summary: He says the studio group became a clique only because producers asked for the players on earlier hits, and discusses guessing hits.

segments.title: Head arrangements in the studio
segments.summary: Songs were built from a singer's bare outline and the band made arrangements on the spot, as they already did on stage.

segments.title: Replacing Earl Palmer and the search for a drummer
segments.summary: The studio group tried June Gardner, Ed Blackwell and others but they were not versatile enough after Palmer left.

segments.title: Charles Williams versus Earl Palmer
segments.summary: He contrasts Palmer's steady time with Charles 'Hungry' Williams, who did unorthodox things and brought humor to his playing.

segments.title: Professor Longhair in the studio and at the Caledonia
segments.summary: He tells how Longhair kicked the piano leg for time and had to be given a Coca-Cola crate in the studio, and recalls Caledonia breaks.

segments.title: The original Caledonia and the in crowd
segments.summary: He describes the dimly lit Caledonia and the late-night in crowd, and the clubs where the musicians hung out.

segments.title: Java, Al Hirt's hit and first BMI royalties
segments.summary: Java did nothing until Al Hirt covered it; Tyler got no royalties until a BMI office found him while on tour with Little Richard.

segments.title: Java's credits and the RCA instrumental album
segments.summary: He explains the three-way credit with Toussaint and 'Friday', and that the songs were made up in the studio for producer Danny Kessler.

segments.title: Snake Eyes on his Ace album and no pay
segments.summary: Toussaint helped him put tunes together; he says he never got money from the Ace album song Snake Eyes released by Johnny Vincent.

segments.title: Forming AFO as a production company
segments.summary: Studio players Lastie, Battiste, Montrell, Beatty, Boudreaux and Tyler formed a production company and partnered with Juggy Murray.

segments.title: Barbara George's hit, Juggy Murray and AFO's pride
segments.summary: AFO had hits with Prince La La and Barbara George until Murray bought her contract and froze their releases; Tyler still counts AFO a success.

segments.title: AFO's philosophy and how members were chosen
segments.summary: They believed they could produce good records and members were chosen for their session histories.

segments.title: John Boudreaux becomes AFO's drummer over Smokey Johnson
segments.summary: Tyler replaced his Joy Tavern band's drummer Smokey Johnson with Boudreaux so AFO members could work together.

segments.title: Tyler's role in AFO and how decisions were made
segments.summary: He screened songs and artists, Lastie handled the books, and decisions were informal.

segments.title: Prince La La and Barbara George come to AFO
segments.summary: Jesse Hill brought Prince La La and Barbara George to the group.

segments.title: End of AFO: the Los Angeles trip and Sam Cooke
segments.summary: After Murray cut them off, a trip to a Los Angeles disc-jockey convention turned into a stay, with Sam Cooke giving them a rehearsal studio.

segments.title: Remarrying in 1956 to Audrey
segments.summary: He says he remarried around 1956 to Audrey Johnson.

segments.title: Expelled from the black musicians' union
segments.summary: He, Earl Palmer and others challenged the black union over unaccounted money; the president was impeached but they were fined.

segments.title: Longshoreman, liquor sales and the Glazer job
segments.summary: Union trouble led him to work three years as a longshoreman, then liquor sales, then drug wholesaler sales until about 1990.

segments.title: Loading ships on the Puerto Rico boat
segments.summary: He describes longshoreman work loading flour sacks.

segments.chapter: Later labels, jazz and the union
segments.title: Parlo Records and Tell It Like It Is
segments.summary: He co-founded Parlo Records with George Davis and Warren Parker and played baritone on the session.

segments.chapter: Later labels, jazz and the union
segments.title: Modern jazz sessions, Compendium and Monkey Puzzle
segments.summary: AFO also produced modern jazz, with Cannonball Adderley and Harold Battiste's Compendium, which Tyler says was ahead of its time.

segments.chapter: Later labels, jazz and the union
segments.title: Never playing in a parade band
segments.summary: He says he never wanted to play or march in brass bands, preferring jazz.

segments.chapter: Later labels, jazz and the union
segments.title: Photo with Sam Cooke from the Louisiana Weekly
segments.summary: The interviewer shows a newspaper photo; the transcript of Tyler's answer is garbled.

segments.chapter: Later labels, jazz and the union
segments.title: 1952 union expulsion article and the union's power
segments.summary: The interviewer shows an article on the expulsions; Tyler repeats the outcome and says the union checked cards at sessions and gigs.
